chapters.synopsisKo: 배고픈 피노키오는 집 안을 뒤져 달걀 하나를 찾지만, 껍질에서 병아리가 태어나 날아가자 자신의 선택을 후회한다.
chapters.narrationDirection: Play the hunger with growing physical comedy, make the discovery of the egg feel miraculous, give the chick bright polite confidence, and end with sincere regret rather than mockery.
chapters.artBrief: Geppetto's humble kitchen-room in a wide paper-theatre panorama: painted fireplace and painted pot, empty drawers, one white egg in the sweepings, a small pan over coals, and an open window through which a yellow chick can fly.

foundation: Night came, and Pinocchio became very hungry.
The pot over the fire was only painted.
He searched every drawer, but found no food.
At last, he discovered one white egg.
He put the egg into a hot pan.
A yellow chick jumped out of the shell.
The chick thanked him and flew away.
Still hungry, Pinocchio wished Geppetto were home.
core: As darkness arrived, Pinocchio's empty stomach became painfully hungry.
He reached for the pot above the fire, only to discover it was painted.
He searched boxes, drawers, and even under the bed without finding food.
Just when he felt hopeless, he spotted a white egg among the sweepings.
Delighted, he planned the perfect omelet and heated a small pan.
When the shell cracked, a cheerful yellow chick appeared instead of breakfast.
The chick politely thanked Pinocchio for opening its shell.
Then it spread its wings and escaped through the open window.
Pinocchio stared at the empty shell while his hunger grew worse.
Remembering the Cricket's warning, he regretted leaving his father.
studio: Nightfall replaced Pinocchio's brief guilt with a hunger that swelled until it seemed as fierce as a bear.
He hurried to the steaming pot above the fireplace, only to learn that both flame and supper were painted illusions.
Boxes, drawers, and the space beneath the bed yielded nothing—not even a crust that a dog might refuse.
Then, among the sweepings, he discovered a single white egg and greeted it as though fortune had returned.
He debated every possible recipe before settling proudly on an omelet cooked in his tiny pan.
But when the shell opened, a fluffy yellow chick stepped out in place of the expected white and yolk.
With perfect manners, the chick thanked Pinocchio for saving it the work of breaking free.
It flew through the window, leaving the marionette frozen with two empty shell halves in his hands.
His imagined feast had vanished, and the hunger he had tried to outsmart now felt more severe than ever.
For the first time that night, Pinocchio admitted that obedience and his father's care might have protected him.

chapters.titleEn: The Night of the Burned Feet
chapters.synopsisKo: 폭풍우 속에서 먹을 것을 구하지 못한 피노키오는 젖은 채 돌아와 난로에 발을 올리고 잠들었다가 두 발을 모두 잃는다.
chapters.narrationDirection: Make the storm vivid but storybook-safe, keep the cold-water prank brisk, then slow down during the dangerous sleep so the consequence feels inevitable rather than graphic.
chapters.artBrief: A connected night panorama: stormy village street on one side, an old man's high window at center, and Geppetto's dark room with a small stove on the other. Lightning, pouring water, wet wooden footprints, and the first dawn light guide the camera.

foundation: Pinocchio went outside to find bread.
The night was dark, cold, and stormy.
He rang a village doorbell for help.
An old man poured cold water on him.
Pinocchio returned home wet and tired.
He put his wooden feet near the stove.
He fell asleep, and his feet burned away.
At dawn, Geppetto knocked on the door.
core: Although the storm frightened him, hunger drove Pinocchio toward the village.
The streets were dark, empty, and shaken by thunder and wind.
He rang a bell and begged an old man for a piece of bread.
Thinking it was a prank, the man poured icy water from the window.
Pinocchio reached home soaked, exhausted, and hungrier than before.
He sat beside the stove and stretched out his wooden feet to dry.
Weariness overcame him, and he fell into a deep sleep.
While he snored, the wooden feet slowly blackened and turned to ash.
He slept through the danger without understanding what he had lost.
At sunrise, a familiar knock and Geppetto's voice woke him.
studio: A violent storm darkened the village, yet Pinocchio's hunger proved stronger than his fear of thunder and lightning.
He crossed the deserted streets until he found a house whose bell he could pull in desperation.
From a high window, an old man heard his request for bread but mistook him for a midnight troublemaker.
Instead of food, a sheet of icy water fell over Pinocchio's wooden head and shoulders.
He stumbled home soaked, weak, and no closer to quieting his empty stomach.
Unable to remain standing, he rested his wooden feet beside the little stove and surrendered to sleep.
The warmth that first seemed comforting became dangerous while the exhausted marionette continued to snore.
Slowly, his feet blackened and crumbled into ash, though he noticed nothing at all.
The night ended with a consequence produced not by magic, but by hunger, carelessness, and fatigue.
At dawn, a knock brought the voice Pinocchio most needed to hear: Geppetto had returned.

chapters.synopsisKo: 제페토는 발을 잃고 굶주린 피노키오를 돌보며 자신의 아침인 배 세 개를 모두 나누어 주고, 피노키오는 아끼는 법을 배운다.
chapters.narrationDirection: Start with clumsy physical comedy, then make Geppetto's care unmistakably tender. Let the pear sequence stay playful while revealing sacrifice and gratitude.
chapters.artBrief: Geppetto's morning room with the locked door and small window, Pinocchio on the floor without feet, Geppetto climbing in, and a table holding three pears, their skins, and their cores. Warm sunrise should replace the previous chapter's storm shadows.

foundation: Pinocchio tried to open the door.
Without feet, he fell to the floor.
Geppetto climbed through the window.
He felt sorry and held his wooden son.
Geppetto gave him three breakfast pears.
Pinocchio demanded that he peel them.
Soon he ate the skins and cores too.
He learned not to waste simple food.
core: Hearing Geppetto outside, Pinocchio tried to stand and fell heavily.
Because he could not open the door, his father climbed through the window.
Geppetto's anger disappeared when he saw that the wooden feet were truly gone.
Pinocchio poured out the entire confused story of his terrible night.
Understanding only that his son was hungry, Geppetto offered three pears.
They had been his own breakfast, but he gave them away gladly.
Pinocchio refused the fruit until his patient father peeled it.
After eating the pears, he discovered that he was still hungry.
With no other food available, he ate every skin and core he had rejected.
Geppetto reminded him that simple things may become precious when life changes.
studio: Pinocchio heard his father's knock and tried to leap up, only to crash to the floor because his feet were gone.
Convinced at first that another trick was delaying him, Geppetto climbed through the window to enter the house.
The sight of his helpless wooden son dissolved his anger into sorrow and immediate tenderness.
Pinocchio then poured the storm, the Cricket, the chick, and the stove into one breathless and confused confession.
Geppetto understood little of the explanation except the fact that the child before him was desperately hungry.
He produced three pears intended for his own breakfast and offered all of them without hesitation.
Still fussy, Pinocchio insisted that each pear be peeled and pushed the skins and cores aside.
Hunger soon defeated pride, and he gradually ate every part he had declared useless.
The small meal revealed the difference between Geppetto's practical love and Pinocchio's changing appetite.
Once satisfied, the marionette finally understood why nothing simple should be wasted or despised.

chapters.titleEn: New Feet and an A-B-C Book
chapters.synopsisKo: 제페토는 피노키오에게 새 발과 옷을 만들어 주고, 추운 날 자신의 외투를 팔아 학교에 필요한 알파벳 책까지 마련한다.
chapters.narrationDirection: Let Pinocchio's promises sound eager but immature, make the crafting sequence bright and tactile, and slow down for the coat revelation so Geppetto's sacrifice lands without sentimentality.
chapters.artBrief: A warm workshop-home panorama: unfinished wooden feet and glue on the table, Pinocchio jumping in a paper suit with bark shoes, a water bowl used as a mirror, an empty coat hook, and Geppetto returning through a cold doorway with the A-B-C book.

foundation: Pinocchio begged for two new feet.
He promised to study and behave.
Geppetto carved and glued the feet.
Pinocchio jumped happily around the room.
Geppetto made him simple paper clothes.
But Pinocchio still needed a schoolbook.
Geppetto sold his only coat to buy it.
Pinocchio understood and hugged his father.
core: After eating, Pinocchio begged Geppetto to replace his burned feet.
He promised to attend school, study hard, and care for his father.
Although he doubted the familiar promises, Geppetto's heart softened.
He carved two strong new feet and attached them with melted glue.
Pinocchio leaped around the room, delighted to stand again.
Because they were poor, Geppetto made clothes from paper, bark, and dough.
The proud puppet admired himself, then remembered he needed an A-B-C book.
Neither father nor son had any money to buy one.
Geppetto went outside and returned with the book but without his coat.
Realizing the sacrifice, Pinocchio embraced and kissed his father.
studio: Once his hunger was satisfied, Pinocchio immediately began to demand a new pair of feet.
He promised school, study, honest work, and lifelong support with all the confidence of a child who wanted something.
Geppetto recognized the familiar performance, yet the sight of his unhappy son softened every attempt at sternness.
With an artist's care, he carved two nimble feet and joined them so neatly that the seams almost disappeared.
The restored marionette sprang from the table and celebrated as though joy itself had entered his wooden legs.
Lacking money, Geppetto fashioned a suit from flowered paper, shoes from bark, and a tiny cap from dough.
Pinocchio admired the gentleman in his water-bowl reflection before remembering the schoolbook his promises required.
The simple request exposed their poverty, for neither of them possessed even a single coin.
Geppetto returned from the winter street carrying the A-B-C book while his patched coat had vanished.
When he claimed the day was too warm, Pinocchio understood the loving lie and covered his father with grateful kisses.
